A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SemTrace and code-recall study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of ten LLMs on CRUXEval and SemTrace, including positional effects, retrieval experiments, line-removal sensitivity, and control ablations.

after.justification: V3 retains original ten-model evaluations, line-removal results, Python-interpreter measurements, and SemTrace analyses. Retained results qualify as original empirical outcomes.

M1.justification: SemTrace retains randomized, independent list assignments using arithmetic operations. The counterfactual sensitivity procedure and normalized degradation formula are unchanged. Higher-digit SemTrace variants already appeared in v1; v3's expanded explanations do not introduce a new method.

E1.justification: V3 removes single-line lexical retrieval, narrowing the task coverage while retaining function retrieval. Python, CRUXEval input/output prediction, SemTrace, CodeSearchNet distractors, and GPT 4.1's higher-digit test scenarios remain covered.

E2.justification: All ten LLMs and the Python-interpreter reference remain represented overall. However, the corresponding SemTrace partial-match comparison shrinks from ten models in v1 Figure 3 to six frontier models in v3 Figure 8; the four smaller models' partial-match curves are absent.

E3.justification: Core sample sizes, distractor counts, eleven positions, greedy decoding, and GPT subsampling remain unchanged. V3 drops the auxiliary prompting/key controls and extends maximum-normalized reporting to lexical recall and SemTrace plots. Its stated context ceiling becomes approximately 16k tokens versus v1 Appendix G's approximately 31k; unchanged distractor settings do not establish an actual budget reduction or rerun.

E4.justification: V3 removes both control ablations from v1 Appendices C–D: disabling query-aware contextualization and testing hexadecimal keys' effect on code understanding. These examined potential confounds in the recall comparison. Higher-digit arithmetic, interpreter sensitivity, partial-match analysis, and unresolved-output analysis are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions use greedy decoding and report bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for line-removal trend fits. No repeated-run counts, seeds, significance tests, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures are introduced; the retained uncertainty reporting practice is unchanged.

E6.justification: V3 removes line-level retrieval results, both control-ablation result sets, and smaller-model partial-match curves. It newly reports aggregate summaries, including 92.73% versus 53.36% median maximum degradation at 80 distractors. Retained baseline table values and corresponding curve shapes match v1 after normalization. V3's new blanket statement that frontier retrieval accuracy exceeds 95% overstates the retained results.

T1.justification: V3 removes v1's formal Code Reasoning Framework: the mixing function, granularity and concentration definitions, performance factorization, and positional expectation in Equations 1–4. The sensitivity formula survives as v3 Equation 1, alongside the existing SemTrace guessing-probability argument. This substantially reduces the formal framework without changing the implemented method.

C1.justification: V3 drops retrieval-granularity dependence as a main contribution and centers the lexical-versus-semantic dissociation. The abstract and introduction strengthen v1's cautious suggestion that benchmarks may underestimate difficulties into claims that models rely heavily on pattern-matching shortcuts and that evaluations substantially underestimate semantic-recall failures.

C2.justification: V3 develops stronger shortcut and arithmetic-memorization explanations and interprets partial matches as gradual recall failure rather than complete breakdown. Section 7 adds specific language, distractor, task, arithmetic, context-length, and benchmark-scale limitations. Conversely, v1's architectural discussion, prompting-dependent interpretation, and explicit limitations concerning dispersed code and reasoning models disappear.

D1.justification: V3 removes the model-architecture/configuration table, line-retrieval prompt, and checklist statements describing an open-source reproduction repository and README. This changes available documentation, not established resource availability. Hardware, software versions, inference access, execution-time estimates, and prompts for retained tasks remain documented.

R1.justification: Related work is rebuilt around long-context evaluation, positional bias, and memorization. Additions include Hartmann et al. on memorization, Wu et al. on counterfactual tasks, Huang et al.'s MATH-perturb, and Winskel on operational semantics. Much of v1's code-slicing, code-generation, and attention-architecture positioning is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conceptual exposition, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves forward, experimental setup becomes a separate section, and results follow a dissociation-and-shortcuts narrative instead of four research questions. Appendices are reorganized, the checklist disappears, and the title changes from Code Reasoning to Code Understanding.

P2.justification: V3 switches to two-column layout and combines frontier-model recall comparisons in Figure 2, with smaller models separated into appendix figures. Lexical and SemTrace plots adopt relative scales; the interpreter plot moves into the main text. Baseline and licensing tables are split, while line-retrieval, ablation, architecture, and absolute-accuracy displays are removed.

improvement.justification: V3's integrated figures and expanded limitations improve readability and scope disclosure. However, it removes controls testing confounds in the central recall comparison while presenting the unchanged higher-digit experiment as more conclusive evidence of arithmetic memorization. The overbroad claim of greater-than-95% frontier retrieval accuracy adds a reporting problem. These losses in evidential support and claim accuracy outweigh the presentation gains.
